chapter: Working with Duke and final reflections
title: 'There is no black music'
summary: Whaley says music is music everywhere, Beethoven was black, and Hinton adds that sound, not sight or color, matters.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Stop thinking of it as black music -- there's no black music. Music is music, all over the world, if you can read them notes, you're all right. Same over there in India, they have music, but it ain't black.
They didn't call Beethoven's music black, did they? Beethoven was a black man.
That's right -- his grandfather was black.
Sure. That's why I say there is no black music -- it's music all over the world.
That's the most rewarding thing I have heard you say, and we've got to stop thinking in terms of color.
Music is a universal art in which
we all participate -- you sitting here, having lost your sight, and me sitting here with my sight -- sight has nothing to do with sound.
It's how you sound. I can recognize you by the sound of your voice, and you recognize me from the sound of my voice -- and not by the color of my skin, because you can't see the color of my skin.
But if you did, it wouldn't make any difference.
No -- that's what I say. Music is -- I tell everybody at the Guild, I bawl some of those guys out. And I just thought about something.
